Summary:
When the Civil War ended in 1865, more than 460,000 newly freed people lived in Georgia. Reconstruction, which lasted until 1871 in Georgia and until 1877 elsewhere in the South, was the struggle over what their freedom would mean.
For a few years, change came quickly. Freed people sought out schools and built all-Black churches. In Atlanta, 37 Black delegates helped write the state constitution of 1868, which provided for Black voting and free public schools. That year, 32 Black Republicans won seats in the Georgia legislature, including Henry McNeal Turner. White legislators expelled them in September 1868, and they were not reinstated until 1870. The Ku Klux Klan targeted Black leaders, and white conservative Democrats held full control of the state by January 1872.
South-View's founders lived through these years. Jacob McKinley built his businesses during Reconstruction, George W. Graham became one of the first two African Americans elected to the Atlanta City Council in 1871, and Robert Grant co-founded Zion Hill Baptist Church in 1872. In 1877, Atlanta's city council ordered the remains of those buried in Oakland Cemetery's "Slave Square" moved. Nine years later, formerly enslaved African Americans founded South-View.
People in this story: Henry McNeal Turner: elected to the Georgia House of Representatives in 1868; Robert Grant: co-founded Zion Hill Baptist Church in 1872; George W. Graham: one of the first two African Americans elected to the Atlanta City Council, in 1871; Jacob McKinley: built his businesses during Reconstruction (buried at Oakland Cemetery)
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), pp. 18–21; Bragg, "Reconstruction in Georgia," New Georgia Encyclopedia; Angell, "Henry McNeal Turner (1834–1915)," New Georgia Encyclopedia; Georgia Historical Society, "South-View Cemetery" marker; LMC 3403 Project 2 Information Sheet (Warren et al., Historical Map group)

Summary:
On October 26, 1885, Albert Watts buried his father in Rest Haven, Westview Cemetery's segregated section for African Americans. The funeral carriages had to enter through the cemetery's back gate. Black Atlantans had faced the same treatment at Oakland Cemetery, where in 1877 the city ordered the graves in the segregated "Slave Square" moved.
In February 1886, Watts and five other African American businessmen petitioned the city for a new cemetery, "a respectable place for Christian burials." The petition was approved that April, and South-View was chartered on 25 acres. It was open to people of any race, but it was owned and run by African Americans, who could now decide how their own dead were buried.
South-View operated as a stockholder corporation from the start, making it one of the oldest African American-owned corporate enterprises in the United States. It has grown from 25 acres to more than 100 and is still an active cemetery.
People in this story: Albert Watts: founder and first treasurer; Robert Grant: founder; John Render: founder; George W. Graham: founder; Charles H. Morgan: founder, bought the first three shares and died three days later; Jacob McKinley: founder (buried at Oakland Cemetery); Nicodemus Holmes: South-View's first president
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), pp. 1–22; Georgia Historical Society, "South-View Cemetery" marker; Bond, "From Enslavement to Legacy: The History Buried at South-View Cemetery," Capital B Atlanta (2026); LMC 3403 Project 2 Information Sheet (Warren et al., Historical Map group)

Summary:
The Panic of 1893 set off a depression that lasted until 1897. Hundreds of banks and thousands of businesses failed across the country, and unemployment stayed above ten percent for five or six years in a row.
South-View's officers had to keep a young cemetery running through it. On August 7, 1893, president Nicodemus Holmes and the board asked the Atlanta City Council to waive the cemetery's $100 license fee, since South-View was small and most of its burials were of the poor. The council said no. South-View survived, and during the Panic it buried about two-thirds of Atlanta's African American dead.
The city paid less to bury Black paupers than white ones. By 1900, South-View was providing pauper graves for $1.35 each, while white pauper burials cost the city at least $2.00. When South-View raised its bid to $2 for equal pay, the city gave the contract to another cemetery that charged $1.50.
People in this story: Nicodemus Holmes: South-View's first president, who led the petition for tax relief; Mitchell Cargile: lost a hearse in the Panic when he could not pay its mortgage; Lucius L. Lee: undertaker who handled many of South-View's earliest burials; David T. Howard: undertaker who later won the city's pauper-burial contract
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), pp. 27, 45–49; "The Depression of 1893," EH.net Encyclopedia; "The Great Panic of 1893," History in the Margins; LMC 3403 Project 2 Information Sheet (Warren et al., Historical Map group)

Summary:
Early on May 17, 1902, in Atlanta's Pittsburgh neighborhood, Will Richardson, a Black store owner, fired on Samuel A. Kerlin, a white former police officer who had arrested him. Officers, neighbors and a growing armed white crowd surrounded Richardson's grocery at McDaniel and Amy streets, where he and several other men had barricaded themselves.
The siege lasted for hours, with an estimated 3,000 or more shots fired, and the store was set on fire. Nine people died: four African American men, four white police officers and a white civilian. James Harrison was shot by the crowd as he tried to escape. Milton Risdon was wounded and arrested.
Within hours, about 15,000 white Atlantans came to see the scene and looted the ruins. The governor sent state militia to patrol Pittsburgh for several days.
People in this story: Will Richardson: killed when his store burned; James Harrison: shot by the crowd as he fled; Milton Risdon: wounded and arrested, later buried beside Richardson at South-View
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), pp. 116–117; Hartzog, "Negro's Deadly Aim," The Bamberg Herald (May 22, 1902); National Register of Historic Places nomination, Pittsburgh Historic District (2006); LMC 3403 Project 2 Information Sheet (Warren et al., Historical Map group)

Summary:
In the summer of 1906, Atlanta newspapers printed sensational and unsupported stories of Black men attacking white women, while both candidates for governor campaigned on segregation and on limiting Black voting. On September 22, after reports of four more alleged assaults, none of them substantiated, a mob of about 10,000 armed white men and boys rioted through downtown. They wrecked Black-owned businesses, dragged people from streetcars and beat or killed African Americans they found on the street.
Rain broke up the downtown mob early on September 23, but the violence moved to Brownsville, a Black neighborhood south of downtown that was home to Clark University and Gammon Theological Seminary. On September 24, after a gunfight in which a white police officer died, state militia entered Brownsville and arrested more than 250 Black men, including professors.
Historians estimate that 25 to 40 African Americans were killed. South-View became the resting place of several of them, and of community leaders who survived the violence or worked to rebuild afterward. In 2006, on the 100th anniversary, a memorial service was held at George Union Wilder's grave at South-View.
People in this story: J. W. E. Bowen: opened Gammon Theological Seminary to people fleeing the mob, then was beaten and arrested by police; Luther Judson Price: arrested on a charge of supplying ammunition to Brownsville residents, later dropped; Alonzo Herndon: the mob smashed the windows of his Peachtree Street barbershop; Henry Hugh Proctor: afterward helped form the Interracial Committee of Atlanta; Peter James Bryant: hosted the ministers who formed the Christian Civic League; William F. Penn: asked white leaders on September 25 how a Black man could be protected in the South; John Wesley Dobbs: guarded his household with a revolver through the nights of violence; Moses Amos: police warned him to close his drugstore because they could not protect it; Henry McNeal Turner: urged Black Atlantans to arm themselves in self-defense; William H. Crogman: helped restore calm afterward; David T. Howard: was called to South Atlanta to collect a riot victim's body; George Union Wilder: a 70-year-old Union Army veteran killed in Brownsville; Frank Smith: a 19-year-old Western Union messenger killed by the mob on September 22; Marshall Carter: a 13-year-old schoolboy who died of his injuries on September 22; Stinson Ferguson: 25, shot on the first night of violence
Sources: Henderson, South-View: An African American City of the Dead (2018), pp. 118–139; LMC 3403 Project 2 Information Sheet (Warren et al., Historical Map group)

Summary:
Atlanta was one of the centers of the movement. On March 9, 1960, students from the city's historically Black colleges published "An Appeal for Human Rights" in local newspapers, and on March 15 they began sit-ins at ten lunch counters and cafeterias.
On October 19, 1960, more than fifty demonstrators were arrested at the Magnolia Room restaurant in Rich's Department Store, among them Martin Luther King Jr. and A. D. King. Atlanta's stores desegregated in October 1961, after the city's public schools were integrated.
Many of the movement's leaders, organizers and supporters are buried at South-View.
People in this story: Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.: arrested at Rich's in 1960; A. D. King: arrested at Rich's in 1960; Martin Luther King Sr.; Fred C. Bennette Jr.; Samuel Woodrow Williams; Ruby Doris Smith Robinson; Julian Bond; John Lewis; T. M. Alexander; William Holmes Borders; Harold I. Bearden; Irene Dobbs Jackson: first African American to receive an Atlanta Public Library card, in 1961; Dorothy Alexander; Bennie McLendon
Sources: "Atlanta Sit-ins," New Georgia Encyclopedia; LMC 3403 Project 2 Information Sheet (Warren et al., Historical Map group)

Summary:
Between 1979 and 1981, about 29 young African American children, teenagers and young adults were abducted and killed in Atlanta. The disappearances began in July 1979. Grieving parents formed the Committee to Stop Children's Murders in April 1980, and the Atlanta Police Department created a Missing and Murdered Task Force that August. The FBI joined the investigation that fall, under Special Agent in Charge John Glover, the first African American to head an FBI field office.
In May 1981, officers watching a Chattahoochee River bridge stopped Wayne Williams, who was arrested that June. He was convicted of two of the murders, both of adults, and was named the primary suspect in most of the others. Critics have questioned whether he was responsible for all of the deaths attributed to him.
The families of seven of the young people chose South-View as their resting place.
People in this story: Milton Harvey: 7 years old; Yusef Bell: 9 years old; Aaron Wyche; Aaron Jackson; Patrick Rogers; Curtis Walker: 13 years old; William Barrett: 17 years old
